advocate.argument: This is a genuine constitutional confrontation: Nepal's Supreme Court, in a rare emergency plenary session, has publicly rebuked the executive over the warrantless midnight arrest of a former Chief Justice, Cholendra Shamsher Rana. That is an unusual institutional escalation, not just a political spat, and it's compounded by the Judges' Society's separate objection, Nepali Congress calling the government's explanations contradictory, and the National Human Rights Commission alleging police blocked its monitors from seeing Rana. Together these signal a widening rule-of-law crisis touching judicial independence, police conduct, and government transparency simultaneously. Nepal Wire can add value beyond the wire reports already circulating (Setopati, OnlineKhabar, Kathmandu Post, Ratopati, Nepalnews) by consolidating the fragmented institutional reactions into one clear timeline: the Sept 26 midnight detention, the 10-hour hold at Teku, the release, and the cascade of objections from the court, judges' body, NHRC and opposition, while flagging the still-undisclosed legal basis for the arrest and RSP's conspicuous silence as an open reporting gap worth chasing with public records/officials today.

skeptic.argument: The core of this story is one official document — the Supreme Court's own press release via spokesperson Koirala — echoed almost verbatim by at least eight Nepali outlets (Nagarik, OnlineKhabar x2, Setopati, Nepal Press x2, DC Nepal, Annapurna Post) within a two-hour window on Sept 28. That is not independent corroboration of an 'institutional cascade,' it's one statement rippling through the wire. The advocate's strongest supporting claims — NHRC being blocked from meeting Rana, Nepali Congress's formal objection, an English-language nepalnews/Kathmandu Post/Ratopati writeup — all sit outside the candidate set and I could not verify them (search access failed repeatedly). Until those are confirmed against primary sources, treat them as unconfirmed additions, not established fact. One candidate in the set literally documents a major party's silence, undercutting the 'multiple institutions piling on' framing. No candidate contains any government or police rebuttal explaining the legal basis for the arrest, so publishing now risks a one-sided account of a serious allegation against the executive. Finally, by the time Nepal Wire would run this on Sept 29, the story has already saturated Nepali media for roughly a day — this is confirmation, not a scoop.

skeptic.argument: The core problem is quantitative conflation. Multiple sources I checked (Republica, Radio Nepal, and the original Republica NEA damage story) explicitly attribute the Rs 74 billion power-sector damage figure to the Bhote Koshi floods of August 26 — a full month before the Asoj 8-11 event this story is nominally about. Kathmandu Post's Aug 30 coverage even says NEA itself later floated losses 'running into hundreds of billions,' meaning the 74bn figure may already be stale and superseded. Splicing an old-disaster damage number into a new-disaster death toll update, under one headline that implies a single causal chain, is exactly the kind of claim-ownership violation the newsroom rules warn against. Separately, the 27-dead/1,065-families cumulative Asoj-8 count and the 21-dead/272-incident rolling 24-hour NDRRMA count are different measurement windows from different agencies; presenting them as complementary risks readers concluding there were 48 total deaths. Individually each underlying fact is well-sourced and attributed, but the synthesis the story proposes — stitching an unrelated August damage estimate onto a September death toll — is the sort of thing a rival outlet or NEA itself could publicly correct. This is an incremental monsoon update, not breaking news, and the power-damage hook is borrowed from an older story.
